28, 1967) is an American former professional [[basketball]] player who played in the [[National Basketball Association]] (NBA). As a [[small forward]], Rice was a three-time [[NBA All-Star]] and made 1,559 [[three-point field goal]]s during his 15-year career. Rice played [[college basketball]] for the [[Michigan Wolverines basketball|Michigan Wolverines]], and was selected by the [[Miami Heat]] with the fourth overall pick in the [[1989 NBA draft]]. He won an [[NCAA Division I men's basketball championship|NCAA championship]] in 1989 and an NBA [[NBA champion|champion]]ship in 2000. In recent years, Rice has taken up [[mixed martial arts]] fight promotion as owner of G-Force Fights based in [[Miami, Florida]], and is an [[NBA scout]] and team ambassador for the Miami Heat. He is the father of [[Glen Rice Jr.]] ==Early life== Glen Anthony Rice Sr. was born on May 28, 1967, in [[Jacksonville, Arkansas]]. He and his family moved to [[Benton, Arkansas]] when Rice was only a few months old. While they lived in Benton, Rice attended both Angie Grant elementary school and Howard Perrin elementary school. When Rice was 12, the family moved to [[Flint, Michigan]].{{Cite web |title=Glen Anthony Rice (1967–) |url=https://encyclopediaofarkansas.net/entries/glen-anthony-rice-13522/ |access-date=2025-07-31 |website=Encyclopedia of Arkansas |language=en-US}} Rice was a star on the [[Flint Northwestern High School]] record setting 1984 and 1985 varsity basketball teams. Rice lead those teams to a combined 55-1 record and consecutive Class A Michigan state titles. After graduating high school in 1985, Rice enrolled at the [[University of Michigan]].{{Cite web |title=Rice, Glen – Greater Flint Area Sports Hall of Fame |url=https://gfashof.org/inductee/rice-glen/ |access-date=January 15, 2026 |language=en-US}}{{Cite web |title=Flint Northwestern High School Boys Basketball – 1984-85 – Greater Flint Area Sports Hall of Fame |url=https://gfashof.org/inductee/flint-northwestern-high-school-boys-basketball-1984-85/ |access-date=January 15, 2026 |language=en-US}} ==College career== Rice played [[college basketball]] for the [[University of Michigan]] [[Michigan Wolverines|Wolverines]] for four seasons (1985–1989), a starter for three of those seasons. He became the school's all-time leading scorer with 2,442 points. He led Michigan to the [[1989 NCAA Division I men's basketball tournament|1989]] [[NCAA Men's Division I Basketball Championship]], scoring an [[National Collegiate Athletic Association|NCAA]]-record 184 points in tournament play, a record that still stands.{{cite news|url=https://query.nytimes.com/gst/fullpage.html?res=950DE6DF173AF937A35757C0A96F948260|title=Rice claims scoring mark|access-date=February 25, 2007 | work=The New York Times | date=April 4, 1989}}{{cite web|url=http://www.cbssports.com/collegebasketball/mayhem/history/tournindyrec|title=NCAA Tournament Records|access-date=February 8, 2010}} Rice was also voted the tournament's [[NCAA basketball tournament Most Outstanding Player|Most Outstanding Player]] and was part of the Associated Press All-America second-team, after averaging 25.6 points for the season, while shooting 58% from the floor and 52% from three-point range. After Rice's junior year, he was invited to try out for the 1988 United States Olympic basketball team, but he was cut before reaching the group of 48.{{cite news|url=https://query.nytimes.com/gst/fullpage.html?res=940DE2DF143CF930A15756C0A96E948260|title=Thompson makes cuts|access-date=February 25, 2007 | work=The New York Times | date=May 23, 1988}} On February 20, 2005, Rice's No. 41 jersey was retired during a ceremony at Michigan's [[Crisler Arena]].{{cite web| url=http://www.michigandaily.com/content/blue-retires-rices-jerseyl| work=The Michigan Daily| last=Holman| first=Josh |date=February 21, 2005 |title=Blue retires Rice's jersey| access-date=February 25, 2007}} Rice made the cover of ''Sports Illustrated'' on April 10, 1989.{{cite news| url=http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/vault/cover/featured/9167/index.htm| archive-url=https://archive.today/20120715113534/http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/vault/cover/featured/9167/index.htm| url-status=dead| archive-date=July 15, 2012| title=On the Cover: Glen Rice| access-date=February 4, 2010 | work=CNN}} In 2026, Rice was inducted into the [[National Collegiate Basketball Hall of Fame]]. He became the third Wolverine to ever earn the honor, joining head coach [[John Beilein]] and [[Cazzie Russell]].{{cite web|url=https://www.mlive.com/wolverines/basketball/2026/07/third-wolverine-will-be-inducted-into-college-basketball-hall-of-fame.html|publisher=[[MLive.com]]|author=Kahn, Andrew|title= Third Wolverine will be inducted into College Basketball Hall of Fame}} Rice continues to rank among Michigan's all-time leaders in several statistical categories, including: *1st in men's career points (2,442) *1st in single-season points (949 in the 1988–89 season) *1st in single-season field goals made (363 in the 1988–89 season) *1st in single-season field goal attempts (629 in the 1988–89 season) *1st in single-season three-point field goal percent (51.6% in the 1988–89 season) *2nd in career field goals made (1,003) *2nd in single-season three-point field goals made (99 in the 1988–89 season){{cite web|title=Men's Basketball Statistic Archive Query Page |publisher=University of Michigan |url=http://stats.ath.umich.edu/basketball/basketstart.php |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100418044313/http://stats.ath.umich.edu/basketball/basketstart.php |archive-date=April 18, 2010 }} ==Professional career== Rice started his senior season as a projected mid-first-round selection, but his stock rose due to his record-breaking performance in the NCAA Tournament, and he was selected #4 overall in the [[1989 NBA draft]] by the [[1989–90 Miami Heat season|Miami Heat]]. ===Miami Heat (1989–1995)=== The Heat was an expansion team in the NBA and was now in their second-year in need of some offensive help after finishing last in the NBA in points per game in [[1988–89 NBA season|1988–89]]. Joining other young players such as [[Sherman Douglas]] and [[Rony Seikaly]], Rice would be called upon to deliver some of the scoring load despite being a rookie. Starting in 60 games, Rice averaged 13.6 points per game his rookie season just behind Douglas and Seikaly, but the lottery-bound Heat only won 18 games. The following year only saw modest improvement for the team from 18 wins to 24 wins, but Rice started in every game he played and increased his scoring load to 17.4 points a game while leading the team in three-point field goals with 71. The [[1991–92 NBA season|1991–92 season]] would prove to be a breakthrough season for Rice and the Heat, as the team improved to 38 wins and featured other young players such as [[Steve Smith (basketball)|Steve Smith]] and [[Brian Shaw (basketball)|Brian Shaw]]. By now Rice had become the team's leading scorer and averaged 22.3 points a game with 155 three-point field goals (second in the league), leading the Heat to its [[1992 NBA Playoffs|first playoff series]] in which the young team was swept by the defending champion [[1991–92 Chicago Bulls season|Chicago Bulls]] led by [[Michael Jordan]]. Despite this, the Heat won fewer games the [[1992–93 NBA season|following year]], while Rice's scoring average slipped to 19 as the scoring load of Seikaly and Smith increased. Rice averaged 21.1 points a game in the [[1993–94 NBA season|1993–94 season]] and led the Heat back into the [[1994 NBA Playoffs|playoffs]] and to their first-ever playoff game win against the [[1993–94 Atlanta Hawks season|Atlanta Hawks]], but the Heat were unable to win the hard-fought first-round series in which the Hawks prevailed 3 games to 2. In the [[1994–95 NBA season|1994–95 season]], Rice averaged 22.3 points a game (10th in the league) and made 185 three-point shots (6th in the league). Despite not being selected to play in the annual [[NBA All-Star Game]], Rice participated in the [[NBA All-Star Weekend Three-Point Shootout|NBA All-Star Long Distance Shootout]] at the [[1995 NBA All-Star Game|1995 All-Star game in Phoenix]], and won the contest, edging out another sharp-shooter, [[Reggie Miller]]. Later during the season in a nationally televised game against [[Shaquille O'Neal]] and the [[1994–95 Orlando Magic season|Orlando Magic]] he scored a career-high 56 points on 20 of 27 shots from the floor including 7 three-pointers. The 56 points were an NBA season-high for the [[1994–95 NBA season|1994–95 season]]. Despite his success, the Heat was unable to make the playoffs. ===Charlotte Hornets (1995–1999)=== Days before the start of the [[1995–96 NBA season|1995–96 season]], newly hired Coach/GM [[Pat Riley#Miami Heat (1995–present)|Pat Riley]] organized a trade in which Rice was sent to the [[1995–96 Charlotte Hornets season|Charlotte Hornets]] along with [[Matt Geiger]] in exchange for disgruntled Hornets center [[Alonzo Mourning]] who had refused any contract negotiations. The Hornets paired Rice with high scoring forward [[Larry Johnson (basketball, born 1969)|Larry Johnson]], and the two led the team to 41 wins. Rice led the team in scoring with 21.6 points a game and led his team in three-point field goals (171) and three-point shooting percentage (42%). He was also named to play in the [[1996 NBA All-Star Game]], but the Hornets failed to make the playoffs. It would be the [[1996–97 NBA season|1996–97 season]] in which Rice would earn the distinction of an elite player in the league. The Hornets had acquired veteran players [[Vlade Divac]] and [[Anthony Mason (basketball)|Anthony Mason]] and no longer featured Johnson, and also hiring a new head coach and NBA legend [[Dave Cowens]]. Rice averaged 26.8 points a game during the season, placing him third in the league in scoring while leading the league in three-point shooting (47%) and minutes played. His play earned him his second straight All-Star Game election, and at the [[1997 NBA All-Star Game]] set an individual [[NBA All-Star Game records#Individual|All-Star game records]] of 20 points in the third quarter and 24 points in the second half to finish with 26 points for the game. His 8–11 shooting performance including 4–5 three-pointer shooting and his 20 points in the third quarter broke Philadelphia guard [[Hal Greer]]'s record (19), set in 1968. By scoring 24 in a half, Rice surpassed the previous mark of 23, owned by [[Wilt Chamberlain]] and [[Tom Chambers (basketball)|Tom Chambers]].{{cite web| url=http://www.nba.com/allstar2007/1997_allstar.html| title=1997 NBA All-Star Game| website=[[NBA.com]]| access-date=February 15, 2007}} Rice's performance is listed on the NBA's 57 Memorable All-Star Moments.{{cite web| url=http://www.nba.com/allstar2008/57allstar_moments/1990s.html| title=57 Memorable All-Star Moments| website=[[NBA.com]]| access-date=February 4, 2010}} His performance helped the Eastern Conference win the game, and earned him the [[NBA All-Star Game Most Valuable Player Award]]. The Hornets won 54 games, and made it into the [[1997 NBA Playoffs|1997 Playoffs]] where they were swept 3–0 by the [[1996–97 New York Knicks season|New York Knicks]] in the first round. Rice would average 22.3 points a game (8th in the league) during the [[1997–98 NBA season|1997–98 season]], finishing second in the league in minutes played and scoring 16 points in the [[1998 NBA All-Star Game]]. The Hornets won 51 games, and in the first round of the [[1998 NBA Playoffs|1998 Playoffs]], they managed to win a playoff series, defeating the [[1997–98 Atlanta Hawks season|Atlanta Hawks]] before losing to the defending champion [[1997–98 Chicago Bulls season|Chicago Bulls]] in the second round. The [[1998–99 NBA season|1998–99 season]] would start late and last only 50 games per team due to a league lockout, and on March 10, 1999, the Hornets traded Rice to the [[1998–99 Los Angeles Lakers season|Los Angeles Lakers]]. ===Los Angeles Lakers (1999–2000)=== [[File:Jalen Rose with the Indiana Pacers.jpg|thumb|Rice defending [[Jalen Rose]].]] In 1999, Rice was again traded in exchange for fan favorite, [[Eddie Jones (basketball)|Eddie Jones]] and [[Elden Campbell]]. The trade did not immediately sit well with Laker fans but Rice was considered the last piece of the puzzle for the Lakers to return to the [[NBA Finals]].{{cite web| url=http://www.thefreelibrary.com/LAKERS'+TRADE+PAYS+OFF%3B+EX-HORNET+RICE+STINGS+HIS+OLD+TEAM+LAKERS+87,...-a083393732| title=Ex-Hornet Rice stings his old team| access-date=February 7, 2010}}{{cite news| url=http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/basketball/nba/news/2001/05/26/sayitaintso_lakers/| title=Say it ain't so: Laker transactions that broke our heart| access-date=February 7, 2010| work=CNN| archive-date=February 7, 2012| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120207001526/http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/basketball/nba/news/2001/05/26/sayitaintso_lakers/| url-status=dead}} Rice was leaving a Hornets team in turmoil with many players demanding trades coming out of a 4-month [[1998–99 NBA lockout#Lockout|lockout]].{{cite news| url=http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/vault/article/magazine/MAG1015203/index.htm| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110604054431/http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/vault/article/magazine/MAG1015203/index.htm| url-status=dead| archive-date=June 4, 2011| title=SI Vault: George Shinn should sell the Hornets before he completely ruins them| access-date=February 7, 2010 | work=CNN | date=March 1, 1999}} [[Dave Cowens|Coach Cowens]] had resigned, [[Anthony Mason (basketball)|Anthony Mason]] was out for the year, Rice was coming back from an elbow injury that he needed to have surgery on, and the owner was in legal trouble.{{cite web| url=http://www.sportsecyclopedia.com/nba/charhorn/charhornets.html| title=Charlotte Hornets History| access-date=February 4, 2010}} The trade to the Lakers made Rice the third scorer behind [[Shaquille O'Neal]] and [[Kobe Bryant]], a trio that general manager and Laker legend [[Jerry West]] envisioned would bring Los Angeles another NBA championship. The Lakers were swept by the [[1998–99 San Antonio Spurs season|San Antonio Spurs]] in the [[1999 NBA Playoffs|1999 Playoffs]], but Rice averaged 18 points per game. Before the [[1999–2000 NBA season|1999–2000 season]], the Lakers hired head coach [[Phil Jackson]], who had won 6 NBA Championships with the Chicago Bulls teams that featured Michael Jordan and [[Scottie Pippen]]. The Lakers also acquired veterans such as [[Ron Harper]], [[A.C. Green]], as well as Rice's former Miami teammates [[John Salley]] and [[Brian Shaw (basketball)|Brian Shaw]]. Led by the play of O'Neal, who won the MVP award for the season, and the all-star play of Bryant, the Lakers won 67 games for first place in the Western Conference. Rice started in 80 games and averaged 15.9 points as the team's third option with 84 three-point shots to lead the Lakers. In the [[2000 NBA Playoffs|2000 Playoffs]], Rice averaged 12.4 points per game while shooting 41 percent from beyond the three-point arc, a career-best for the playoffs. The Lakers defeated the [[1999–2000 Sacramento Kings season|Sacramento Kings]], [[1999–2000 Phoenix Suns season|Phoenix Suns]], and [[1999–2000 Portland Trail Blazers season|Portland Trail Blazers]] in the first three rounds of the playoffs en route to advancing to the [[2000 NBA Finals]] to play the [[1999–2000 Indiana Pacers season|Indiana Pacers]]. In the second game of the Finals, Bryant suffered an ankle injury, and Rice scored 21 points to help the Lakers take a 2–0 lead in the series. Rice would average 11.5 points a game for the series, including 16 points with 3 shots from three-point range in Game 6 as the Lakers defeated the Pacers 4 games to 2 to give Rice his first and only NBA championship. Although the Lakers had won the championship, a lot of drama had unfolded behind the scenes between Rice, head coach Phil Jackson and GM Jerry West since the time between getting swept by the Spurs and the eventual championship.{{cite web| url=http://www.forumblueandgold.com/2009/01/15/the-curious-career-of-glen-rice/| title=The Curious Career of Glen Rice| date=January 15, 2009| access-date=January 15, 2009}}{{cite news| url=http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/basketball/nba/2000/playoffs/news/2000/06/13/lakers_pacers_pre_ap/| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060209041944/http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/basketball/nba/2000/playoffs/news/2000/06/13/lakers_pacers_pre_ap| url-status=dead| archive-date=February 9, 2006| title=Rice, Jackson continue war of words| access-date=February 4, 2010 | work=CNN}} There was a report that Rice was upset when the Lakers exercised a $7-million option for 1999–2000 instead of letting him become a free agent.{{cite news| url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1999-dec-20-sp-45740-story.html| title=Life at the Top Looks Good for Lakers...but Below Surface Rice Issue Is Simmering| access-date=February 4, 2010 | work=Los Angeles Times | first=Tim | last=Kawakami | date=December 20, 1999}} Shaquille O'Neal, Rice's close friend, believed that Rice was the pure shooter he needed to keep teams from double- and triple-teaming him in the playoffs, and felt partly responsible for bringing Rice to the Lakers (and trading Eddie Jones to do it). Rice was eventually traded to the [[2000–01 New York Knicks season|New York Knicks]]. ===New York Knicks (2000–2001)=== In New York, Rice would take on a sixth-man role on the team and provide the Knicks with well-needed support off the bench. In the [[2000–01 NBA season|2000–01 season]] he played in 72 games, averaging 12 points-per-game. Rice made 25 starts, averaging 14.2 points and 5.2 rebounds in those games and led the Knicks in scoring 9 times.{{cite web| url=http://www.nba.com/playerfile/glen_rice/bio.html| title=NBA.COM: Glen Rice Bio| website=[[NBA.com]]| access-date=February 7, 2010}} While Rice's defense is often singled out as the reason for his departure, he ranks 145th among all-time NBA players in career steals (958).{{cite web| url=https://www.basketball-reference.com/leaders/stl_career.html| title=NBA & ABA Career Leaders and Records for Steals| access-date=February 7, 2010}} His tenure with the Knicks lasted only one year, as he was hobbled by a foot injury (plantar fasciitis) and was unable to find a niche in New York behind [[Allan Houston]] and [[Latrell Sprewell]].{{cite news| url=https://www.nytimes.com/2001/08/12/sports/pro-basketball-notebook-trading-rice-a-knicks-overreaction.html/| title=NOTEBOOK; Trading Rice a Knicks Overreaction| access-date=February 4, 2010 | work=The New York Times| date=August 12, 2001| last1=Wise| first1=Mike}} After the season in which the Knicks lost in five games to the [[2000–01 Toronto Raptors season|Toronto Raptors]] in the first round of the [[2001 NBA Playoffs|2001 Playoffs]], he would eventually be traded to the [[2001–02 Houston Rockets season|Houston Rockets]] for [[Shandon Anderson]]. ===Houston Rockets (2001–2003)=== In Houston, Rice joined a young team featuring [[Steve Francis]] and [[Cuttino Mobley]] and was initially excited about returning to a starting role after being relegated to more of a third-option with both the Lakers and Knicks. Things started slowly in Houston as Rice was still on the mend, rehabbing from his foot injury which limited him to just 20 games in the [[2001–02 NBA season|2001–02 season]]. The following year, he would manage to play in 62 games including 26 starts to average 9 points a game for a Rockets team that now featured center [[Yao Ming]]. Following the [[2002–03 NBA season|2003 season]] he would be traded to the [[2003–04 Utah Jazz season|Utah Jazz]] for [[John Amaechi]], but would then sign with the [[2003–04 Los Angeles Clippers season|Los Angeles Clippers]]. ===Los Angeles Clippers (2003–2004)=== A knee injury (partially torn tendon) ultimately derailed and eventually brought Rice's career to an end. In his final season with the Clippers, he became the 48th player in NBA history to score 18,000 career points. Fittingly, it was on February 18, 2004, against the Lakers, and he would retire after playing just 18 games. == NBA career statistics == {{NBA player statistics legend|champion=y|leader=y|record=y}}
